message.content:
## Decision
Do not deploy this. Official docs make Node.js's Permission Model a blast-radius limiter for trusted code, not a tenant sandbox: it "does not protect against malicious code" and is a "seat belt," while SECURITY.md states it is "not ... a security boundary against intentional misuse or a compromised process" ([permissions.html#permissions](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permissions); [SECURITY.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/node/v24.21.0/SECURITY.md#permission-model-boundaries-permission)). Customer-uploaded JavaScript therefore needs OS-level isolation (separate OS users, containers, seccomp/AppArmor) — which SECURITY.md explicitly assigns to the operator.

## Assumptions to change
1. **Wildcard scope.** Wildcards truncate: "/home/*.js will work similar to /home/*". `--allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js` grants all of `/srv/jobs`, not just `.js` ([permissions.html#file-system-permissions](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#file-system-permissions)).
2. **Symlinks.** "Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files and directories"; granted paths must contain no relative symlinks ([limitations-and-known-issues](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#limitations-and-known-issues)).
3. **Pre-opened fd.** "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model" ([constraints](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permission-model-constraints)).
4. **`--env-file`.** It is read before initialization and is "not subject to the rules of the Permission Model"; its variables, including `NODE_OPTIONS`, "are parsed and applied," and that variable accepts `--allow-fs-read`/`--allow-worker` ([cli.html#--env-filefile](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/cli.html#--env-filefile); [#node_optionsoptions](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/cli.html#node_optionsoptions)). Treat any writability of that file/environment as permission-granting.
5. **Staging signal.** `--permission-audit` never denies and publishes only diagnostics-channel events, so staging cannot evidence enforce-mode behavior; combined with `--allow-*`, only ungranted scopes are audited ([audit-mode](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#audit-mode)).

## Worker inheritance: conflicting
[constraints](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permission-model-constraints) says "The model does not inherit to a worker thread"; SECURITY.md says workers inherit the parent's restrictions and modified `execArgv` grants nothing. **UNVERIFIED** — resolve via the v24.21.0 worker-permission tests/source or a Node.js issue before relying on `--allow-worker`.

## Useful for trusted code
`process.permission.has()`/`drop()` to shrink grants after init (whole-scope for wildcards, irreversible), and audit diagnostics channels for discovery ([runtime-api](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#runtime-api)). Worker options otherwise inherit by default ([worker_threads](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/worker_threads.html#new-workerfilename-options)).

**Certification:** No — neither document supports certifying tenant isolation.
message.reasoning_content:
Now I have enough for the core answer. Key documented facts:

1. permissions.html: "This feature does not protect against malicious code... seat belt approach" — permission model is not a security boundary against malicious code; SECURITY.md "Permission Model Boundaries" section: designed to reduce blast radius of mistakes in trusted application code, not a security boundary against intentional misuse.

2. Env file: "The Permission Model is initialized after the Node.js environment is set up. However, certain flags such as --env-file or --openssl-config are designed to read files before environment initialization. As a result, such flags are not subject to the rules of the Permission Model." So --env-file bypasses the model — but that's the launcher reading it, not the job; still means env file read is not constrained. Actually the concern: they load env file outside the read list; docs confirm that works (not subject to PM). But also means the tenant can potentially via NODE_OPTIONS in env file? Actually --env-file variables parsed and applied including NODE_OPTIONS. That's a risk: if the env file is attacker-influenced... Actually the job itself could maybe not set env. But NODE_OPTIONS from env file is applied and NODE_OPTIONS allows --allow-fs-read etc. Hmm, but the env file is loaded by the launcher, not by the untrusted script. Still worth noting that --env-file is not subject to PM and env vars configuring Node.js (NODE_OPTIONS) are parsed and applied — so anything able to influence that file or env can grant permissions. Documented: cli.html --env-file: "The environment variables which configure Node.js, such as NODE_OPTIONS, are parsed and applied." And cli.html says --allow-fs-read etc are allowed in NODE_OPTIONS. So that's a real escalation path to flag.

3. FD passing: "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model." So passing an already-open fd bypasses the model.

4. Wildcards: --allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js — "After passing a wildcard character (*) all subsequent characters will be ignored. For example: /home/*.js will work similar to /home/*." So the literal /srv/jobs/*.js grants read to everything under /srv/jobs (prefix match), not just .js files. Also the automatic wildcard addition for existing directories. Either way, the read grant is broader than intended.

5. Symlinks: "Symbolic links will be followed even to locations outside of the set of paths that access has been granted to. Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files and directories." So relative symlinks in job dirs are an escalation. SECURITY.md says realpath resolution before permission check is intended behavior; symlinks resolving to allowed path are not a bypass — that's about allowed path. Both consistent-ish: permissions.html warns symlinks followed outside granted set.

6. Worker inheritance conflict: permissions.html constraint: "The model does not inherit to a worker thread." SECURITY.md: "Workers inherit the permission restrictions of their parent process. Passing an empty or modified execArgv to a worker does not grant it additional permissions." Conflicting. worker_threads.html says workers inherit non-process-specific options by default; execArgv default inherited from parent thread — but that's about Worker options, not permission enforcement. Both permissions.html and SECURITY.md are official; they conflict → mark UNVERIFIED. Resolution target: Node.js worker_threads/CLI docs source or the permission-model test suite in node test/parallel (e.g., test-permission-worker-threads.js) at v24.21.0 — but I shouldn't overreach; suggest a pinned source/issue.

Also: --permission-audit added in v24.20.0 — exists in v24.21.0, fine. Also "If both --permission and --permission-audit are specified, --permission takes precedence." Staging with audit mode granting allowances: audit mode combined with allow flags audits a subset. Note audit mode only logs; no denial, so staging results don't prove deny-mode behavior. Also audit does not require --permission.

Also --allow-worker: grants ability to create workers in the main process; docs don't say the worker then gets restricted set (conflict above).

Also note: file system restriction only covers node:fs; "It does not guarantee that users will not be able to access the file system through other means, such as through the node:sqlite module." And SQLite ATTACH DATABASE reads files with process privileges (SECURITY.md). Also process._debugProcess() ungated. Also Run-Time Loadable Extensions, OpenSSL STORE.

Also: for the job, entrypoint implicit read is included — fine.

Answer structure ≤400 words. Include a decision, corrections, useful mechanisms, limitation, certification answer.

Recommendation: don't use PM as sole isolation; use OS-level isolation (separate OS users, containers, seccomp/AppArmor) per permissions.html process._debugProcess section; PM as defense-in-depth for trusted code. Use process.permission.has/drop for defense-in-depth in trusted code; --allow-fs-read absolute explicit paths, no wildcards; put job dirs without symlinks; pass data via pipes not fds... actually can't rely on fd.

Decision: Do not deploy as designed. The docs state the Permission Model is a "seat belt" for trusted code and "does not protect against malicious code"; SECURITY.md says it is "not ... a security boundary against intentional misuse or a compromised process." Customer-uploaded JS requires OS-level isolation.

Corrections:
1. Sole boundary — false premise. (permissions.html#permissions; SECURITY.md Permission Model Boundaries)
2. Tenant isolation cannot be certified by these docs — no; both sources disclaim guarantees.
3. --allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js: wildcards truncate — "/home/*.js will work similar to /home/*", so this grants all of /srv/jobs, not just .js. [permissions.html#file-system-permissions]
4. Relative symlinks in job dirs: documented "Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files and directories"; must ensure granted paths contain no relative symlinks. [permissions.html#limitations-and-known-issues]
5. Pre-opened fd: "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model." So the passed fd is deliberately outside the model.
6. --env-file: read before PM init, "not subject to the rules of the Permission Model"; and env vars including NODE_OPTIONS are parsed/applied — NODE_OPTIONS accepts --allow-fs-read/--allow-worker, so any influence over that file/env grants permissions. [permissions.html#permission-model-constraints; cli.html#--env-filefile; cli.html#node_optionsoptions]

7. Worker inheritance conflict: permissions.html says "The model does not inherit to a worker thread"; SECURITY.md says workers inherit parent restrictions and modified execArgv grants nothing. Contradiction → UNVERIFIED. Resolve against v24.21.0 worker-thread permission tests/source or an issue; do not rely on --allow-worker as an inheritance guarantee.

Also audit-mode premise: --permission-audit never denies, so staging cannot validate enforce-mode outcomes; staging with --allow-* also audits only the ungranted subset. Note that --permission-audit is v24.20.0+ (fine in v24.21.0).

Useful for trusted code: process.permission.has()/drop() to shrink grants after init (docs: drop is irreversible, whole-scope for wildcards); audit diagnostics channels for discovering required grants. FD passing: not a boundary.

Certify? No.

Then remaining: --allow-worker grants worker creation only; --allow-child-process propagates flags via NODE_OPTIONS in v24.4.0+.
